#7407. Creators who show their sources build trust, survey finds

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Journalist-led research found audiences increased trust when news videos identified their sources, such as government documents and interviews.

RELATED ARTICLETwo-thirds of news influencers are men — and most have never worked for a news organizationSarah ScireNovember 18, 2024About one in five U.S. adults regularly gets their news from news creators on social media platforms, but it can be difficult for audiences to suss out which personalities to trust amid an avalanche of misinformation, hot takes, and polarizing content.

New research spearheaded by a team of journalists and political scientists shows that giving audiences a peek into the reporting process can help bolster their trust in the news.

Proof News, a nonprofit newsroom focused on tech accountability, in collaboration with researchers at the French university Sciences Po, shared social news videos with 2,000 U.S. adults to measure their perceptions of trustworthiness. Participants were randomly assigned one of Proof’s yet-to-be-published short-form news videos.

Some participants viewed videos with labels describing the sources, others saw videos with labels describing the newsroom’s ethical standards, and some saw videos without a label. The Sources labels appeared on cards embedded at the end of the video, like a credits reel, or were placed into the video description, the text accompanying the video.

Participants then rated the videos on various trust metrics. We found that labeling videos did increase trust — particularly a label that described the video sources in the description and, to a slightly lesser extent, a label describing newsroom standards in the credits.

This effect was particularly prominent among survey respondents who identified as Democrats or reported having high trust in science. Those groups, when shown the sourcing label in the description of a general news video, reported higher assessments of transparency and trust in the journalist.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with labels for text articles, but Sally Lehrman, founder of The Trust Project, said the findings were still intriguing.

“I’m excited to see the results,” Lehrman said. “Methods and references really do resonate…People are asking, where did the journalist get this information, and how can I trust it.”

As audiences increasingly turn to social media for news, there is a growing public discussion about how trustworthy creators are, especially when it comes to disclosing their funding and relationships. In January, The Wall Street Journal wrote about corporate and foreign interests using influencers to push agendas. In August, The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon secretly hired conservative military veterans with large online audiences to amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s messaging, and a New York Times investigation revealed online influencers received funding from political campaigns without disclosing the connection in their videos.

Some creators have begun trying to distinguish themselves from this type of behavior through their own disclosure efforts.

RELATED ARTICLEWith Local News International, Dave Jorgenson becomes his own TikTok guyNeel DhaneshaSeptember 9, 2025Journalist and creator Dave Jorgenson, who has nearly 1 million followers across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram, has started publishing a transparency report on his website, Local News International, revealing his sources of funding alongside his editorial standards.

Ultimately, he thinks disclosures of political funding should no longer be voluntary but mandatory. “Platforms should be regulating themselves,” Jorgenson said in an interview. “You can’t really force that unless there are laws.”

Proof used Jorgenson’s ethics and transparency statement as a model for the newsroom standards label in video testing and found that it increased viewers’ trust in the news outlet and the likelihood that they would share a general news story.

New York City is already considering disclosure requirements in the wake of revelations in the Columbia Journalism Review that exposed the inner workings of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s connections with influencers. The author of the article, Anya Schiffrin, a senior lecturer at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, testified at a September city council meeting that creator relationships — both paid and unpaid — should be disclosed to viewers.

“It’s important for democracy that we have standards,” Schiffrin said.

RELATED ARTICLEProof News is Julia Angwin’s attempt to bring the scientific method to investigative journalismNeel DhaneshaMarch 21, 2024Proof News, which launched in 2024, pioneered an Ingredients label that takes cues from the scientific method and names the journalists’ hypothesis, sources, limitations, and the story’s findings.

To test whether the label worked to increase viewer trust for short-form vertical videos, we stripped down the Ingredients label to a bullet list of sources followed by an asterisk denoting the reporting limitations. The survey showed the label had a consistent positive effect when placed in the video description, the text box that is often located under the video.

The team also tested how labels performed on online text news articles. The survey showed 1,600 U.S. participants original, unpublished Proof News stories without a label, with a Proof Ingredients label, a label modeled after the Trust Project that described the reporting process, and a label describing newsroom standards.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with the print labels. The most significant findings were an increase in perception of transparency when the reporting process label was used on a polarizing story and an investigative story.

One possible explanation for the differing results between labeling video and text articles is the “ergonomics” of the medium, said Damien Bol, a professor at the Center for Political Research at Sciences Po who helped lead the survey design and data analysis.

“When reading a text, for example, people can quickly skim through it or skip parts of it, whereas a video forces them to follow the story second by second, even when watching at double speed,” Bol said. Different formats, Bol said, shape the “experience of consuming a news story.”

Earlier this month, Julia Angwin, an author of this article, hosted a private convening of creators at Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy to discuss creating shared standards that could be conveyed through a label or other public statement.

The group of 30 leading content creators from news, science communication, education, history, and other evidence-based fields discussed how they could distinguish their work by signaling to viewers their commitment to standards that could include disclosing funding sources and the use of artificial intelligence. Creator-led efforts to bring this to fruition are ongoing.

San Diego-based journalist Lisa Remillard, who has more than 4 million followers on her TikTok channel “The News Girl,” said that making videos with verified facts can feel like a small club. But if she can’t independently confirm something, she’s “not putting that out there.”

Remillard’s audience appears to appreciate transparency. Earlier this year, she published a video describing her editorial standards — and was richly rewarded for it. “I think clearly defining those ethics and standards resonated with my audience and gave them a reason to want to financially support my work,” Remillard said.

Jessica Yellin, the founder of the political podcast, YouTube channel, and social media brand “News Not Noise,” has also called for news creators to voluntarily sign a Creator Constitution, agreeing to journalistic standards such as citing sources, fixing errors, and disclosing financial relationships.

She said labeling sources is about the “signal.” Even if audiences don’t take the time to digest every word, Yellin observed, “It’s the act of showing it that matters.”

Julia Angwin is the founder of Proof News and the founding director of the Independent Media + Audience Project at the Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School. Annie Gilbertson is managing editor of Proof News. Rina Palta is editor-at-large at Proof News and senior data scientist at the Independent Media + Audience Project.

Julia Angwin is the founder of Proof News and the founding director of the Independent Media + Audience Project at the Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School. Annie Gilbertson is managing editor of Proof News. Rina Palta is editor-at-large at Proof News and senior data scientist at the Independent Media + Audience Project.

#7405. Anthropic: Autonomous Systems Security Engineer

Anthropic’s mission is to create reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems. We want AI to be safe and beneficial for our users and for society as a whole. Our team is a quickly growing group of committed researchers, engineers, policy experts, and business leaders working together to build beneficial AI systems.

Claude is trained and served on hardware in data centers Anthropic operates and in sites partners build and run for us. DCSE secures that footprint: the sites, the hardware moving through them, and the people and vendors who touch it. You'll be the engineer who owns autonomous systems across that footprint as one security domain, from both sides: drones, ground robots and automated vehicles for patrol, inspection and moving hardware, including the security of that automation inside secure areas, and the detection systems that tell us what is flying over or operating near a site uninvited.

You set the approach, select and integrate the platforms and sensors, write the requirements vendors build to, and run what you ship, from the operating model where operators assign missions and machines carry them out to the playbook that turns a detection into an identified track and a well-evidenced handoff to whoever holds authority over the airspace. Interdiction is not part of this role. The goal is security that runs itself: coverage, fleet health and evidence verified continuously, with tools and AI agents doing the routine triage. We favor simple, standard controls and tools that can be verified over elaborate ones. We use Claude throughout our engineering workflow and expect you to as well.

You'll work with the rest of DCSE, including its physical security systems engineers and the engineers on its security monitoring platform, with Anthropic's data center operations and legal teams, and directly with site operators, equipment vendors and aviation and public safety authorities. The role is based in San Francisco, with remote applicants in the US considered, and involves regular travel to data center sites, which are critical infrastructure.

Autonomous security and inspection systems: own the drones, ground robots and other autonomous platforms for perimeter patrol, incident response and infrastructure inspection: platform selection, operating model, operator qualification, maintenance, and the data path from machine to analyst

Tools, automation and AI agents: build the integrations that carry detections, tracks, telemetry and fleet health into the team's security monitoring platform, and the tools and agents that triage detections, check fleet health and assemble evidence. When a review keeps costing people time, you build the tool or agent that retires it

Detection of uncrewed systems: engineer the sensing that tells us what is flying over or operating near a site, what it is and who needs to know: sensor selection and evaluation against live targets, per-site coverage, classification and false-alarm handling, and the playbook from first detection to handoff, with evidence retained

Security of site automation: engineer the controls on automated vehicles, robots and similar machines that move hardware or work inside secure areas: identity and access, network isolation, what they may record and where it goes, fail-secure behavior, their place in chain of custody, and acceptance before they enter a site

Health monitoring: define and test heartbeats, loss-of-coverage and lost-link alarms and fail-secure behavior, so a silent sensor or machine shows as a fault, not a quiet day

Vendor requirements and acceptance: write the requirements, evaluate against live flights and runs, and hold vendors to what they ship

Have engineered autonomous or sensing systems in the field (drones, ground robots, automated vehicles, or RF, radar or optical detection sensors): selected, integrated or secured them for an operation other people relied on, and verified what they actually do against real targets or runs rather than a datasheet

Have integrated systems you did not build (vendor APIs, SDKs, appliances, machine and sensor telemetry) into a platform that outlives any one of them

Read and review code, design the data systems behind security tooling, and build automation (often with AI coding agents) using Git and code review

Remote pilot certification (for example FAA Part 107) and experience flying beyond visual line of sight under a waiver or exemption

“The move toward developing our membership program in the last couple of years has really been about understanding how important it is for us to build more community and to foster that loyalty [of our] audience,” Carey said. “When we were looking at that, it really felt like an app was a good way to continue pointing in that direction.”

Vox isn’t the only news outlet focusing on mobile apps. The Verge — Vox’s former sister publication under Vox Media — named traffic declines as one of the reasons why it plans to launch its own app next year. The Wall Street Journal’s head of digital, Taneth Evans, recently said that the Journal makes its app more useful to users by offering all of its mediums in one place. Evans also said that news publishers “need to give people reasons to open an app beyond simply offering news.”

“Websites will become a service for agents,” Evans said. “Apps are gonna be the thing that humans will connect with.”

Vox declined to provide website traffic numbers, but data from Comscore shows that the website’s unique visitors decreased by 36% year-over-year between September 2025 (7.4 million) and September 2026 (4.8 million). Archived data from SimilarWeb shows the site had 20.8 million visits in September 2021.

“Vox isn’t immune to the larger trends that have led to web traffic declines in recent years, but those only represent a portion of our audience,” Carey said in an email. “Vox is focused on building audience engagement across platforms, with social video views up 86% year-over-year and newsletter audience up 14%.”

“Even if there wasn’t a decline in search traffic, as everyone has been seeing — and we still get members from search — we want to create that relationship with our audience,” publisher and editor-in-chief Swati Sharma said. “People know Vox and they have a relationship with Vox. We have a younger audience that’s on all of these different platforms. I think it is definitely a part of building that relationship ourselves.”

That the app makes all Vox content accessible in one place for current and future members also signals the “un-siloing” of the newsroom overall, Sharma said. Vox currently has 78 editorial employees.

RELATED ARTICLESwati Sharma is leading a new era in Vox’s mission to “explain the world”Hanaa' TameezMay 6, 2021When Sharma, who has helmed Vox.com since 2021, first arrived, she found that Vox’s main mediums (text, audio, and video) “weren’t in service of one another.” The “silos” allowed teams to build their own audiences and products. But while teams discussed story ideas with each other and during editorial meetings, “they all [needed] to go into their creative spaces and find what works for their medium and not be in service of just one larger section.”

That’s changed over the past five years, Sharma said. Each team — text, video, and audio — does a little bit of everything now. Text reporters appear on podcasts and in videos, while podcasters and hosts also write their own newsletters.

“In a lot of newsrooms, there’s one dominant form, and at Vox, there wasn’t. They’re all really important,” Sharma said. “[Senior correspondent] Dylan Scott is on our Unexplainable podcast talking about Alzheimer’s. [Host and editorial director] Astead Herndon does a newsletter and a Substack Live every week, and he does a podcast. That’s the future for us, and that’s where our whole newsroom is moving, where those silos are done and you can basically do everything.”

#7403. Google Ads Are Reaching Upper-Funnel Searches – But AI Mode Pays Less via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Spend less time on publishing and reports, and more on helpful content. November 18, 2 PM ET.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Protect PPC budgets as Google's AI Mode shifts queries up-funnel, with four account changes to test new inventory and prove whether discovery pays.

Google’s head of search data science told advertisers on Oct. 28 that people now come to Google earlier in their buying journeys, asking long, detailed questions that start a long way from a purchase. That same afternoon, Alphabet’s chief business officer told Wall Street that the AI Mode queries driving that shift make Google less money than traditional searches do.

Put those two statements side by side, and you have the planning problem facing every paid search manager heading into 2027. The queries are arriving at the top of the funnel, while most Google Ads accounts are still judged at the bottom.

This column pulls the advertiser lessons out of that conversation, checks its numbers against what Google has published elsewhere, and turns it into four changes you can make in your accounts before Black Friday.

On Google’s Ads Decoded podcast, Oct. 28, host Ginny Marvin opens by saying the show is “getting out of the advertising world and into the organic search world” for the day.

Her guest is Shivani Mohan, Google Vice President of Data Science and User Experience Research (UXR) for Search. Mohan’s UXR teams interview people one-on-one to learn why they phrase questions the way they do, and her data scientists study logs of what billions of users actually do. She started her career designing bicycles, where she says, “you get one shot to really nail the user understanding” (3:04) because a finished product can’t be iterated.

Google can iterate on Search every day. Advertisers, on the other hand, get roughly one shot per budget cycle to convince finance that a channel is working.

See also: Google Data Shows AI Search Users Moved Past Keywords, Your Content Hasn’t

Mohan calls this “an expansionary moment” for search. For most of Google’s history, she explains, people had to translate a curiosity into a keyword. That friction is fading, so “people are asking much longer, much more detailed questions.” More important for keyword lists, she says, “They’re asking net new types of queries that they would have never thought to ask before.”

Marvin asked the question many PPC managers would ask. Are people coming back with follow-ups because the first answer failed?

Mohan said no, and gave a detail I hadn’t heard Google explain before. “In our data science practice, we penalize queries, which we call man refs, manual refinements,” because a user having to add words means Google missed the original intent. By her account, the growth in follow-ups reflects new curiosity rather than bad answers.

For advertisers, that follow-up behavior is no longer just a user experience story. Google says it is launching multi-turn ads in AI Mode in the U.S., so ads can appear in follow-up queries, according to Shashi Thakur, VP and GM of Google Search Ads.

“What we’re seeing more and more of with AI is that people’s queries are kind of moving up the funnel,” Mohan said, with more brainstorming questions and more questions about how to think about a category altogether.

She also described what shoppers do when they get close to a decision. When people compare two products, “they really don’t want to just see the summary.” They want reviews, podcasts, and videos from people in their own circumstances.

See also: How AI Search Trends Are Changing PPC Campaign Structures – Ask A PPC

Mohan says query length has increased three times, and Marvin repeats it in her wrap-up as queries in conversational search “running three times longer on average.” Google’s published version is narrower. Its AI Mode Report (U.S., May 2026), as cited by Thakur, says queries in AI Mode are on average three times longer than traditional searches. That is an AI Mode comparison, not a claim about all Google searches.

Mohan also says, “one in every six searches is multimodal.” Google’s May report put it at more than one in six AI Mode searches in the U.S. And on the Q3 call in October, CEO Sundar Pichai gave a newer, global figure, saying “one in five AI Mode searches globally use voice, images or documents.”

To her credit, Mohan explained how Google vets the numbers it releases. Her team checks that an insight is repeatable, and “we don’t want to be able to put out any number that is at a peak point or is something that is liable to change.”

I take her at her word on that rigor. But the durable number advertisers need most is one Google hasn’t published, which is how ads in AI Mode actually perform. Alphabet’s 10-Q doesn’t break out paid clicks or cost-per-click for AI Mode. The only performance figure in Thakur’s post is that click-through rates are “already similar between sponsored and organic product list items within AI Mode,” based on Google internal data from Aug. 20 to Sept. 3, 2026. That’s two weeks of data, measured by Google, comparing ads to organic listings rather than to traditional Shopping ads. Treat it as Google’s claim until your own accounts confirm it.

See also: How To Leverage AI Ad Placements For Stronger PPC Performance

The podcast and the earnings release went out the same day, and the release is where the up-funnel story gets a price tag.

Alphabet reported Google Search & other revenue of $63.35 billion in Q3 2026, up 12% year-over-year, after growth of 19% in Q1 and 17% in Q2. Sequentially it was nearly flat, up from $63.27 billion in Q2. The 10-Q, filed Oct. 29, shows paid clicks on Google Search & other up 8% year-over-year, down from 13% in each of the first two quarters, while cost-per-click rose 4%.

Meanwhile, Pichai said query growth was the highest it has been in five years, including commercial queries.

When JPMorgan’s Doug Anmuth asked why queries were growing faster than Search revenue, Google’s SVP and Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler pointed first to currency, which he called the largest driver of the slowdown versus Q2. Then he added, “The strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.”

Schindler’s optimistic case lines up neatly with Mohan’s research. “On AI Mode, many of these queries are upper-funnel queries, allowing us to capture new high-value commercial intent,” he said, adding that “the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time.” Google is now scaling ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and queries and expanding AI Mode ads to international markets.

Pichai offered his own historical frame on the call, comparing this moment to the shift to mobile, when Google focused first on the user experience and then on monetization. Anyone who managed paid search in that era remembers how it felt. In Q3 2016, Alphabet reported paid clicks up 33% and cost-per-click down 11%, according to Reuters, as searches moved to smaller screens with cheaper ads.

Here is where I think the analogy breaks. In the mobile transition, the monetization gap showed up as cheaper clicks. This time, cost-per-click is still rising, and the gap shows up as queries growing faster than paid clicks. Advertisers aren’t getting a discount for the move up the funnel. They’re getting new top-of-funnel inventory, priced by the same auction, and the burden of proving it pays off.

Marvin closed the episode with her own takeaways for advertisers, starting with a call to “recalibrate how they’re thinking about search” outside of last-click action. Here is how I’d turn that into work this week.

1. Confirm you’re eligible for the new inventory at all. Marvin reminded listeners that “ads in AI mode and AI overviews are matched to both the query and the content of the AI response.” Google’s help documentation for ads in AI Overviews says that only broad match keywords or keywordless targeting (AI Max for Search, Performance Max, Shopping, and Dynamic Search Ads) can serve ads inside the overview. Exact match can still serve above or below it, and Marvin has clarified that an exact match keyword won’t block the broad match version from triggering inside the overview. If your core non-brand campaigns run exact and phrase only, you’re opting out of the placements Google is scaling. Keep exact match where you need control, and give broad match or AI Max a defined slice of non-brand budget with Smart Bidding and clean conversion data behind it.

2. Fill the six conversational attributes in Merchant Center before Black Friday. Marvin flagged these optional fields, which Google rolled out at Google Marketing Live in May. They are question_and_answer, document_link, related_product, item_group_title, variant_option, and popularity_rank. They don’t affect product approval, and Google recommends adding them through a supplemental data source, so your primary feed stays untouched. Mohan’s point about comparison shoppers wanting real-world detail maps directly to question_and_answer and related_product. Start with your top sellers, since Black Friday falls on Nov. 27 this year.

3. Build a long-query segment in your reporting. Export your search terms report and group terms by word count, for example, one to three words, four to seven, and eight or more. Then compare conversion rate, cost per acquisition or ROAS, and how often each group appears in conversion paths. If the long queries convert poorly on last click but show up as earlier touches, you have the upper-funnel evidence finance will ask for. If they don’t show up anywhere, you’ve found where broad match or AI Max is spending on discovery you can’t yet justify, and you can tighten with negatives and brand controls. Either way, don’t let a blended CPA hide the difference.

4. Fix the page the ad sends people to. Marvin said, “Your ad should position your business as the natural next step in that user journey” and urged advertisers to “focus on reducing post-click friction.” A searcher who typed a 25-word question about a specific situation won’t convert on a generic category page. If you use AI Max’s final URL expansion, Google chooses the landing page from your site, so thin pages get picked for nuanced queries. Audit your highest-spend landing pages for the specifics a follow-up question would ask about, such as comparisons, sizing, pricing, and use cases. As Marvin noted, much of this sits outside the PPC team, so bring in your SEO, content, and CRO counterparts.

Mohan’s bicycle-design lesson applies to advertisers more than she may have intended. Google has the logs, the UXR interviews, and the ability to ship changes daily. Advertisers have the auction bill and a quarterly budget review.

My view is that Google is right about where search behavior is heading and wrong if it expects advertisers to fund that shift on faith. Until Google reports AI Mode ad performance with the same durability standard Mohan described for user statistics, I’d treat AI Mode and AI Overview reach as a test line with its own budget and its own success metric, rather than something that quietly drags down blended CPA.

Google checks its numbers for durability before it publishes them. Your CFO will expect you to do the same.

#7401. Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial new terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media company announced today.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”

Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta plans to consult.

The proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta announced it would push back implementation of its new terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

“We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the new terms are unreasonable,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”

Since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the company withdraw the terms as they’re currently written.

“After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s plans to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the company is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”

On October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade said on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

“We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade said in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”

This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

#7398. The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.

Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the new features:

I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.

The Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main new feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

Say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the new AI feature could account for.

Cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”

But because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.

“What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from New Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”

“This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” says Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”

“Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”

“PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of New York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”

Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”

Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the new AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

Dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

One consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”

Meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the new AI feature because it quickly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” says Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”

ChatGPT Ads is replacing two manual bid caps with average cost targets. Here's what changes for new campaigns, existing campaigns and API partners, and when.

The ChatGPT Ads platform is replacing two manual caps, the maximum bid (Max Bid) and maximum CPC (Max CPC), with average cost targets that advertisers can set as part of their advertising campaign strategy. This is according to an OpenAI help document on the topic of bidding and pricing that was updated on their website Thursday.

Beginning Nov. 9, advertisers creating a conversion campaign, which they are using to hit a specific cost per conversion, get Target CPA in place of Max Bid; likewise, advertisers creating a click campaign beginning Nov. 9 also have the option to use Target CPC. Max Bid and Max CPC will no longer apply to existing campaigns from Jan. 1, 2027.

From Nov. 18, a Max Bid or Max CPC value that an API partner sends through the old fields to create a campaign or change an ad group’s bid type becomes an average target, not a maximum.

OpenAI’s bidding page describes Target CPA and Target CPC as average cost goals rather than limits on each bid. Target CPA is the average of what an advertiser wants to spend on a conversion (such as a purchase or a lead) and Target CPC is the average for a click. In both cases, a single click or conversion may cost more or less than your target, and you may end up paying more or less on average.

For click campaigns, the page compares the new option with the cap it replaces:

“While Max CPC caps individual bids, Target CPC lets our system bid above or below your target in individual auctions, aiming to deliver as many clicks as possible from your budget while working toward your desired average CPC.”

The warning on this page is about a possible restriction on delivery when the target is set below recent performance. An example shows how they calculate a $40 actual CPA using $400 in ad spend and 10 attributed purchases. It points out that if a $20 Target CPA is set it does not mean that the system will be able to deliver purchases at a $20 cost. Additionally, the amount spent by a campaign may fall short of the full budget due to overly restrictive targets or poor conversion data.

This page says the bidding goal and the billing event type are two different settings and therefore, a Target CPA campaign can be optimized for conversions while being charged for clicks or impressions, which depends on how the campaign is being billed.

In August Brooke Osmundson reported that Microsoft would cease to offer Max CPC on new non-portfolio campaigns using a strategy such as Target CPA and Target ROAS beginning Oct. 1. However, existing campaigns and portfolio bid strategies may continue to use it. Microsoft’s official reasoning behind the change is that the setting can interfere with their bidding systems’ ability to perform optimizations toward performance objectives.

API partners are getting their own Target CPA and Target CPC fields, and the old Max Bid and Max CPC fields change behavior on Nov. 18. The bidding page says partners can adopt the new fields once they’re available but doesn’t give a date for them.

OpenAI suggests that the legacy fields be replaced with the new fields starting Nov. 18. Legacy fields will stay active until the end of December; however, if you utilize a field to create a campaign or convert an ad group’s bidding strategy, it switches to Target CPA or Target CPC and the value becomes counted as an average cost instead of a maximum bid.

On Jan. 1, 2027, legacy fields will be deprecated. As such, the page advises partners to have all integrations updated prior to this date.

OpenAI’s bidding page also explains how the price of a winning ad is set:

“The final winning auction bid sets the price you pay.”

That rule applies across all bidding strategies, including existing Max Bid and Max CPC campaigns, the page says.

The company’s advertiser basics page described a relevance-weighted, second-price auction when I read it on Nov. 5. However, that wording is gone after an update, and the page now uses the same pricing rule as the bidding page.

The basics page also still says advertisers set a maximum bid at the ad-group level, and it recommends that CPC campaigns start with a maximum bid of $3 to $5 per click. In April, I covered Digiday’s report that an early version of the ads manager showed CPC bids in that range to some pilot advertisers.

The Maximize results page is still telling advertisers who are required to operate within a bid limit that if they have to do so without an automated process, they can do it using manual or advanced bid controls. Its setup steps say to select Manual: Max bid to use a different strategy. Also, the bidding page gives the old Maximize results strategy a new name, Intelligent bidding.

With Max Bid and Max CPC, advertisers have the ability to limit how much they will bid in each auction. With Target CPA and Target CPC, it is the advertiser who sets both a budget and an average cost; then it is up to the automated bidding systems to set individual bids. Some individual clicks or conversions could come in at higher costs than the targets.

As OpenAI suggests, advertisers should consider setting their targets based upon recent actual CPA or CPC averages. In addition to reviewing the overall spend of the campaign as well as results (clicks, conversions), advertisers should also monitor the actual average cost per click or conversion as the campaign continues to learn. Advertisers who buy through API partners should find out which bid fields those tools use after Nov. 18, since a legacy max-bid value sent to create a campaign will count as an average target.

Target CPA and Target CPC are available in Ads Manager beginning Nov. 9, with advertisers able to move their campaigns from this date forward. The legacy API bid field changes behavior on Nov. 18 and is going away Jan. 1, 2027, which marks the end of Max Bid and Max CPC for those who have yet to switch.

There is no information on OpenAI’s bidding page as to what will be the target of a campaign that is still using Max Bid or Max CPC after the caps retire. By switching prior to retirement, the advertiser is able to set its new target at the time of the switch.

#7394. Only 32% of Americans have high confidence that news orgs will report midterm election results accurately, survey finds

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

About six in 10 Americans said they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a new national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% said they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

The survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that showed trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

The Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

In another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents said journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

#7391. Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

Most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, announced it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

The grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

For many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” said Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money quickly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1

RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” said María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

“They said to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”

First-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, said Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

“It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” said Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”

The Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” said Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

The funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin said. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2

RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”

“Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” said Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”

The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

“The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” said Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased new software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very quickly,” he said, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

The Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a new website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”

The Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a new media kit, which Olson said has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.)

The open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr said. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to plan ahead.

Many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

The Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” said Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the new hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

The Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

The funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz said.

The Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve company housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, said editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3

The turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

Sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” said Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”

The World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr said. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.)

Other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”

EcoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

The salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz said. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”

“At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she said, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”

Beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she said. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

“I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she said, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”

Planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she said.

Ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she said. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”

NotiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” said CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

California’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

In Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

For instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer said, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

Planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak said. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

“The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak said. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”

Anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he said, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

Press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting company Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

The coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants said the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving quickly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4

This was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” said Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear plan. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he said it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

Sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”

In addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin said 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

Stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar said, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

To small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

So several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she said.

Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

Since 2023, Anglin said, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition says it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

When Press Forward first announced the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee said it felt like “a slap in the face.”

“Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin said. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”

The argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher said. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”

Young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

“I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he said. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”)

Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

Young said he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

Right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak said the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health issues in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”

As for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”

LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he said, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”

A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person said, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”

The Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer said.

“I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”

The Sandpoint Reader, Olson said, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”

Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”

“We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she said. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”

#7390. Meta Pauses Its Updated Business And Ad Terms Due Nov. 20 via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Updated business and ad terms won't take effect as scheduled. The ad terms still in force let the company crawl advertisers' sites, including for training.

Meta paused new ad and business terms scheduled to go into effect on Nov. 20. That leaves advertisers and other businesses using Meta’s services operating under existing terms. The pre-existing terms permit Meta to crawl content on advertiser websites for use such as “research and training,” whenever the advertiser places an ad order.

The Meta Business Help Center notice refers to the Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. According to the notice, the updates “are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026.”

On Nov. 5, Nieman Lab reported that Meta had posted the notice regarding halting the updates, and according to a Meta spokesperson, “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”

Meta says the four existing documents stay in effect until further notice. Each one’s page now opens with a line saying the updates are on hold. When I checked on Nov. 10, the U.S. and UK English previews of the updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms showed a “page isn’t available” message.

The Commercial Terms currently in force, dated March 6, 2024, don’t include a crawling paragraph. The paused version would have added one covering sites associated with a business’s products or services. The Commercial Terms apply to any business use, including managing a Facebook Page.

The Self-Serve Ad Terms in force, dated Aug. 22, 2025, already include a crawling grant. By placing an ad order, an advertiser gives Meta the right to “access, index, cache, analyze or crawl” the content on its domains. The listed uses include developing advertising and other business-related products, “research and training,” and maintaining the integrity of Meta’s products.

The Ad Creative Generative AI Terms, dated May 6, 2024, also let Meta crawl URLs that advertisers provide, for use with their ads.

Adweek reported in October that the suspended Commercial Terms included a new section called AI Features. In this section, advertisers would be “solely responsible” for all of the results produced by Meta’s AI features as well as all changes those features make (including features that Meta enables automatically).

In its Ad Creative Generative AI Terms currently in effect, Meta has tied that responsibility to the advertiser’s own actions. The terms say that when an advertiser makes use of or posts AI-generated content, they are “solely responsible” for determining if the Output is correct, and if it is suitable for public display.

According to a Meta spokesperson who spoke to Adweek, advertisers can opt out of individual Advantage+ features at any time from within their Ads Manager account.

Businesses using Meta will not be required to consider any new business or ad terms prior to Nov. 20. For advertisers, the crawling allowance under the current ad terms will continue to apply when an advertiser places a new order; likewise, the terms granting this crawling allowance do not mention robots.txt.

The announcement from Meta says the company has made no changes to its crawling methods. Furthermore, the same options are available to content owners to express their crawl preferences via robots.txt.

Meta’s crawler documentation identifies Meta-ExternalAds for ads and various other business products. Additionally, the documentation identifies Meta-ExternalAgent for uses such as training foundation AI models. The documentation specifically includes robots.txt rules naming both of these crawlers, so review how you currently handle rules for both within your robots.txt file. The same page says two of Meta’s other crawlers might skip robots.txt in certain situations.

Meta says it’s still talking to the parties involved and that it’ll give an update once it has more to share. As of Nov. 10, the announcement hadn’t set a timeline for updating terms, nor had it specified whether or how much of the revised terms would be changed.

Nieman Lab reports that courts in Brazil and Norway have entered preliminary injunctions against these terms based on complaints made by press organizations. According to the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), its investigation is still open. It is investigating both the current terms of business for Meta and proposed changes to those terms. The timelines listed are subject to revision; currently the first phase of fact-gathering is scheduled to run through January 2027.
